bib.title: Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Conversational Systems

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Conversational Systems" (RAGate), Xi Wang (Sheffield), Procheta Sen (Liverpool), Ruizhe Li (Aberdeen), Emine Yilmaz (UCL). arXiv:2407.21712v1 [cs.CL], 31 Jul 2024. Preprint (no venue printed).
COVERAGE: all 12 of 12 pages; 51,131 of 51,131 chars read (body, Tables 1-4, Appendices A-C, references skimmed). Figures 3-4 are bar charts with no extractable numbers; I did not look at the images.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Central claim: always augmenting every turn with retrieval can be unnecessary and harmful. In the paper's example, a generic request ("things to do") gets a narrower, preference-assuming answer with knowledge and a more diverse, natural one without.
  number: none (one GPT-4 illustration, Fig. 1)
  setup: qualitative example only
  quote: "The knowledge-augmented system response is being information conditioned with limited diversity and assuming specific user preferences. In contrast, the system response is more diverse and natural in this early stage of a conversation."
  where: p.1-2, Fig. 1, lines 111-119
- Always-augment improves overlap metrics but lowers generation confidence by about 10%. Confidence is the average of the minimum token probability and is tied to hallucination risk by Varshney 2023.
  number: Aug-All 4,964 turns: BLEU 16.08 vs 9.38 No-Aug; confidence 8.3677 vs 9.3425 (-10.43%)
  setup: KETOD (GPT-2 backbone), BERT-Ranker top-3 knowledge (k=3), gold action in the input, test set
  quote: "Aug-All 4964 16.08 0.3927 0.8258 8.3677 -10.43%"
  where: Table 3, p.6; also "we also identify a significant drop in the model's generation confidence level."
- RAGate-MHA gets most of the always-augment quality with about 16% of the augmentations, and loses little confidence.
  number: 787 of 4,964 turns; BLEU 12.14 (No-Aug 9.38, Aug-All 16.08); confidence -0.36% vs -1.65% for Random-Aug at 787
  setup: as above, BERT-Ranker top-3
  quote: "using RAGate-MHA, which augments 787 system responses, only lowers the average confidence score by 0.36%, instead of the 1.65% when randomly selecting an equal number of turns to augment."
  where: Sec 5.3, p.6
  caveat: the authors say "comparable" to Aug-All, but BLEU is 12.14 vs 16.08, which is a clear gap. ROUGE-L is 0.3882 vs 0.3927.
- The gate beats random selection at equal budget. RAGate-PEFT with 230 augmentations (BLEU 10.45) beats Random-Aug with 787 (BLEU 10.01). Human-label (631 turns) gets BLEU 11.66, confidence -0.93%.
  number: see above
  setup: Table 3
  quote: "the use of RAGate-PEFT, which identifies 230 turns of system responses for knowledge augmentation, can even outperform the random baseline that augments 787 system response turns with improved response quality."
  where: p.6
- Knowledge quality matters. With only the rank-1 snippet, Aug-All's confidence drop shrinks to -2.9%, and RAGate-MHA's confidence rises (+0.37%). The authors read this as "less is more" and as confidence reflecting the relevance of the augmented knowledge.
  number: Aug-All -2.9%; RAGate-MHA +0.37%
  setup: BERT-Ranker rank-1 knowledge. Rank-5 and TF-IDF variants are in Table 4, where Aug-All confidence is 9.0604 at rank-5 and 8.4188 for TF-IDF top-3.
  quote: "Augment-All 4964 16.05 0.3944 0.8259 9.0655 -2.9%"
  where: Table 3 and Table 4 (Appx C)
  caveat: the authors say different amounts and relevance levels have a "marginal effect" on quality metrics. Confidence is the only metric that moves. Rank-5 knowledge gives nearly the same confidence as rank-1 (9.0604 vs 9.0655), which weakens the "confidence tracks relevance" claim.
- The gate task is hard. Prompting Llama-2 zero-shot or in-context fails, and fine-tuning is far better.
  number: best prompt F1 0.1230 (Llama-2-13B zero-shot) vs 0.4082 for QLoRA Llama-2-7B, context only
  setup: KETOD test labels. Positives are only about 12.1% of turns, so precision is low.
  quote: "it can outperform all RAG-Prompt approaches by a big margin (e.g., 0.4082 versus the highest 0.1230 F1 scores)."
  where: Table 2 and Sec 5.1, p.4-5
- The gate classifiers are weak in absolute terms. PEFT is high-precision, low-recall; MHA is the reverse.
  number: MHA([contx⊕resp]) F1 0.4281 (P 0.3500, R 0.5510); MHA(contx) F1 0.4065 (P 0.3210, R 0.5541); PEFT contx-(syn-resp)-ner P 0.6818 but R 0.2321. Llama-2-13B in-context F1 (0.0915) is lower than zero-shot (0.1230).
  setup: 4 heads, 64 embedding, 2-5 layers
  quote: "contx-(syn-resp)-ner 0.6818 0.2321 0.3464"
  where: Table 2
- Adding retrieved knowledge to the gate input hurts classification.
  number: PEFT F1 0.4082 -> 0.1069 with knowledge; MHA 0.4065 -> 0.3636 (concat) and 0.3271 (cross)
  quote: "when we add the retrieved knowledge to the input features for prediction, we observe a significant performance drop across all evaluated aspects."
  where: Sec 5.1
- Where RAGate augments. Human labels cluster at the start of conversations and in domains that need extra information (travel, hotels, trains, flights, services, rental cars) or entity descriptions (movies, music, media, events). MHA tracks this better than PEFT, which under-augments.
  number: none extractable (Figs 3-4)
  where: Sec 5.2
- Weak retrieval baseline: the BERT-Ranker is much better than TF-IDF, but retrieval is poor in absolute terms.
  number: Recall@1 0.2475, Recall@3 0.4714 (BERT-Ranker) vs 0.0227, 0.0871 (TF-IDF)
  setup: context as query
  quote: "BERT-Ranker 0.2475 0.4714"
  where: Table 1
- Small user study: the gate implicitly signals when useful retrieval exists.
  number: 54% of 50 samples
  setup: 50 turns where RAGate-MHA predicted augmentation; the raters were co-authors; 0-4 scale, 3-4 counted as useful
  quote: "We found that in 54% of cases where the prediction was for augmentation, users also found the snippets useful."
  where: Appx B
- Framing (cited, not tested here): retrieval augmentation addresses stale knowledge, hallucination, and domain adaptation. It cites Shuster 2021 for a reduced hallucination rate with DPR.
  quote: "Shuster et al. (2021) demonstrated that using a dense retrieval model (DPR) ... can significantly reduce the hallucination rate, according to a corresponding human evaluation."
  where: Sec 1
- Gate formulation: a binary gate f(ct) or f(ct, et,k) in {0,1} chooses between g(ct, et,k) and g(ct) (Eq. 1). Three variants: prompting (Llama-2 7B/13B), QLoRA fine-tuning (rank 16, Llama-2-7B), and a multi-head-attention encoder.

LIMITS
- Authors concede: only TF-IDF and BERT-Ranker were tried (no dense retrieval such as DPR). No larger LLMs such as GPT-4, owing to compute (one RTX 4090). Little suitable conversational data.
- One dataset: KETOD, a task-oriented dialogue set built on SGD, with 16 domains and a GPT-2 backbone. Only 12.1% of turns carry human "needs knowledge" labels. It is not open-domain chat and not a modern LLM generator. Table 4's caption says "SGD dataset", while the text says KETOD.
- Quality is measured with BLEU, ROUGE and BERTScore against reference responses. There is no human evaluation of the final responses. Confidence is a proxy for hallucination, and no hallucination rate is measured.
- Table 3's caption defines confidence as the "average value over the lowest logit"; the text says minimum token probability. The two are inconsistent.
- The gate's F1 is at most about 0.43, so most gating decisions are wrong. The "human label" is itself a noisy ground truth for "needs RAG".
- The user study is small, uses co-authors as raters, and has no baseline.
- Single run; no seeds or significance tests are reported.
- Dated: Llama-2 and GPT-2 are old, and this predates later adaptive-RAG work.

BUILDS ON
- Retrieval-augmented generation: Lewis et al. 2020, Karpukhin et al. 2020 (DPR), Shuster et al. 2021, Komeili et al. 2022, Li et al. 2022.
- Joint retriever-generator work: Shi et al. 2023, Shen et al. 2023, Kang et al. 2023 (SURGE).
- Knowledge-seeking turn detection: Kim et al. 2020 (DSTC-9), Hong et al. 2023, Jin et al. 2021.
- Confidence and hallucination: Varshney et al. 2023.
- Gate idea from LSTM gates (Graves 2012).
- Methods: QLoRA (Dettmers et al. 2024), LoRA (Hu et al. 2021), the Transformer (Vaswani et al. 2017), Arora et al. 2022 for prompting.
- Data: KETOD (Chen et al. 2022).
- Retrieval-quality framing: Salemi and Zamani 2024, Yu et al. 2024.

CODE: Prompt (Appendix A, zero-shot), verbatim: "Below is an instruction that describes a task. Please respond with 'True' or 'False' only that appropriately completes the request. ### Instruction: Analyse the conversational context so far. Generate an appropriate response. Consider the invovled entites. Estimate if augmenting the response with external knowledge is helpful with an output of 'True' or 'False' only. ### Input: [Converstion Context Input] ### Response:"

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.1): the same conversation answered with and without a knowledge snippet. It shows over-augmentation faster than prose.
- Fig 2 (p.3): the three RAGate variants (prompt, PEFT, MHA encoder).
- Fig 3 (p.5): how often augmentation is chosen by position in the conversation. Humans and RAGate augment mostly early turns.
- Fig 4 (p.6): augmentation counts by domain.
I did not run the figure-captions script. The captions above come from the text.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Extraction is clean apart from the garbled Fig 2 text and the tables, which are flattened to rows. The typo "RAGate-MHA can outperform RAGate-MHA" appears in Sec 5.2 and is probably meant to say PEFT. The Table 3 row label "RAGate-Llama" is the PEFT variant.
